snippet.title: How to Paint Better and Faster | This First House
snippet.description:
Contractor Zack Dettmore shows a homeowner some tips to help him paint better and faster and still achieve professional results.

SUBSCRIBE to This Old House: http://bit.ly/SubscribeThisOldHouse.

Painting is one of those things that anyone can do, but not everyone can do well. Contractor Zack Dettmore showed our homeowner, Jorge, some tips and tricks that professional painters use to work fast and efficiently while still achieving top-quality results.

Sequence Matters
If you want to work efficiently, plan your painting sequence. Zack likes to paint the trim first so if he accidentally paints the wall, the touch-up is much easier. Then, Zack paints the walls before the baseboard as paint rollers often leave a bit of splatter. The baseboards are last, where Zack can easily cover any splatter or drips and get that clean, fresh look.

Unload the Can, Load the Brush
Zack likes to pour as much paint as you can in the roller tray so that the paint can is light and easy to carry. Then, rather than loading the brush with paint and dragging it off on the rim, Zack suggests loading the paint and tapping the excess off on the insides of the can. This helps keep the brush loaded without making a mess.

Tips for Cutting In
When it’s time to cut in, Zack doesn’t like to use tape. His tip for efficient painting is to load the brush, put plenty of paint onto the wall, and then move the paint into the corner with a smooth, steady stroke, flattening out any drips along the way. This applies for walls, ceilings, trim, and anywhere else that requires cutting in.

Clean Up the Paint Roller
Paint rollers are always full of lint and loose fibers. If you don’t remove them, they’ll end up in the paint and on your freshly painted walls. To avoid this, Zack suggests rolling up and down on a strip of painter’s tape to remove those loose bits.

Twirl the Paint Rollers
One of the biggest time-wastes on a painting project revolves around loading the roller, where the painter has to stop painting, bring the roller to the tray, bring it back to the wall, and continue. Zack suggests loading the roller with plenty of paint, and then slowly twirling the roller from the tray to the wall to avoid dripping.

Roll Toward the Arm
When rolling paint onto the wall, you want to move toward the direction of the roller arm. The arm side of the roller will have slightly more pressure, which means the opposite side can feather the paint in and blend it. If the arm is on the right, start on the left side of the wall and work to the right, rolling straight up and down and overlapping the previous past.

snippet.title: Tesla Range Anxiety: After 2.5 Years of EV Ownership Did I Cut it Close?
snippet.description:
After 2.5 years of EV ownership, I didn’t expect to feel this… range anxiety.

This was a short-notice road trip into Mid Wales, an area with no Tesla Superchargers and very limited public EV charging infrastructure , made even more challenging by stormy weather, which significantly reduced efficiency and increased energy consumption throughout the drive.

Driving an EV in heavy rain, strong winds, and colder conditions can have a noticeable impact on range, and on this trip every mile really mattered. With charging options few and far between, this became a genuine real-world test of EV planning, efficiency management, and charging reliability in one of the UK’s more remote regions.

Mid Wales is stunning, but it also highlights the challenges EV drivers can face when you leave well-served routes like the M4, M5, and major A roads, especially when weather conditions work against you.

This isn’t a worst-case scenario, just an honest look at owning and driving an EV in rural UK conditions, where charging access and efficiency both matter.

snippet.title: Chinese vs European Electric Cars: What Should You Go For in 2026? #electriccars #china #europe
snippet.description:
Chinese EVs are getting cheaper, faster and more common across Europe.
And it’s making some European car brands SERIOUSLY nervous.
Because cars from companies like BYD, MG or XPENG often cost thousands less than European competitors, while offering surprisingly modern technology.

So are Chinese electric cars a smart buy in 2026, or are there important compromises people only notice in hindsight?

Yes — definitely. They offer strong value for money, modern technology, and competitive battery systems.

And in many cases, they're pushing the entire market forward.

But they're not automatically the best choice for everyone. If your priorities are long-term reliability, resale value, or a very polished driving experience, then it's worth comparing carefully with more established brands.

In the end, there's no right or wrong decision. It depends on what matters most to YOU.

But one thing is clear: Chinese electric cars are no longer a niche option. They are becoming a SERIOUS part of the European market — and they're changing the competition.

So, what's your take? Would you consider buying a Chinese electric car?

snippet.title: The NEC-Approved Splice I Hate… and the UK Inline Splice I Love
snippet.description:
The NEC-Approved Splice I Hate… and the UK Inline Splice I Love
In this Short I compare a US, NEC-approved in-line NM-B (Romex) splice to a UK inline “click-in” splice. The US connector is legal but clunky; the UK design feels faster, cleaner, and more robust—yet it’s not NEC-compliant in the U.S. Why? We break down listing/labeling requirements (UL/ETL), box/accessibility rules, and 110.3(B) “installed per listing.”
I’ll show both terminations, talk pros/cons, and explain what would have to change for the UK style to be allowed here.

👉 Question for electricians & DIYers: Which would you trust in your walls—and why?

snippet.title: How Much Does It REALLY Cost to Charge an Electric Car?  #goe #electriccars #costs
snippet.description:
How much does it really cost to charge an EV? If you charge your EV at home, it’s usually MUCH cheaper than petrol or diesel.

In the UK, home charging can cost around 25p per kilowatt-hour — and even less with overnight EV tariffs.

In countries with lots of wind or hydropower, like parts of Northern Europe, prices can be even lower.

Public rapid charging is different. That can cost two or even three times more than charging at home. So the smart move is simple: charge at home whenever possible — especially overnight.

▬ Charging capacity ▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬ 
EV chargers - also called wallboxes - usually come in two versions: up to 11 kW or 22 kW. Since most electric cars can only charge with 11 kW AC anyway, an 11 kW wallbox will normally be enough. Even if you own a 22 kW version, your car will still limit charging to 11 kW. So, check what your car supports first – this could save you the decision.

Also, 22 kW wallboxes are more demanding on your home connection and, depending on the country, may need official approval. By contrast, 11 kW versions usually just need to be registered. So unless you specifically need 22 kW, the 11 kW option is the smarter choice.

▬ Mobile or stationary EV charger ▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬ 
Aside from charging capacity, it’s also important to consider where you want to use the wallbox. If you only charge at home, a stationary version makes sense. It’s hard-wired into your electricity supply and must be installed by a professional, as it involves high-voltage connections.
If you’d like to take it with you now and then – for example on trips or to charge at a friend’s house – a mobile wallbox is ideal. A mobile wallbox, like our go-e Charger Gemini flex 2.0 plugs into a red CEE socket, can be unplugged in seconds and stored in the boot. No electrician required.
Also think about where you want to install it: in your garage or somewhere accessible, like your driveway. If it’s public-facing, make sure your EV charger has RFID access so only authorised people can charge. Extra family members or friends simply need their own RFID card or chip. By holding the chip to the go-e Charger after registering it – the person is authorised to charge.

▬ EV charger features▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬ 
Once you’ve decided which charging capacity you need, and whether you’d prefer a stationary or mobile wallbox, the next step is to think about the functions your future wallbox should have.

If you just want straightforward charging – plug in, charge, unplug – a standard wallbox is enough. 

But if you’d like to save money and time, or to take advantage of automation, then I’d recommend buying a wallbox with smart features and Wi-Fi as well as mobile connectivity.

This type of wallbox does cost a bit more than a standard one, but it gives you remote control via app, scheduling, setting charging limits, price caps, PV surplus charging, and loads of automation and integration options.
Take the go-e Charger CORE as an example: You can plan charging times, set a kWh limit, or even define the maximum electricity price you’re willing to pay. If flexible prices rise, the wallbox pauses charging, and resumes when they drop again. This way, you can benefit from flexible electricity tariffs and always charge at the cheapest times. Of course, it will only work if you have a contract with a flexible electricity tariff provider and activate it in the go-e app.

With these features, you can make sure you never pay a penny more than planned and always stay in full control of your charging costs.
And if you have solar panels, even better – you can automatically charge from your own surplus energy instead of feeding it into the grid for a low price and buying it back at a higher price.

If your PV system doesn't generate enough electricity, for example on cloudy days, then the EV charger enables combined charging from both solar and grid power, so you’ll still have the charge you need by the next day. And with phase switching, PV surplus charging becomes even more efficient.

▬ EV charger for techies ▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬ 
The go-e Charger is not only easy to use for beginners, but it is also perfect for more advanced users. Open interfaces such as API, Modbus TCP, MQTT or OCPP mean you can integrate it into your own systems for even greater flexibility.

If you run several chargers at home, make sure yours supports load management – ideally dynamic load management. That way, charging power will automatically be balanced against the available energy in your home and solar system, so your connection is never overloaded.
